Price advocated for abandoning legacy protocols in favor of systems that can be securely updated remotely, noting that while larger manufacturers tend to be more accepting of protocol changes, the industry faces ongoing challenges with unreliable cybersecurity in control systems, potentially necessitating the development of proprietary secure protocols or exclusive use of verified trustworthy systems. 4 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications 2 Legacy Devices For the context of this paper, we define legacy devices as existing devices which are outdated and have been su- perseded by newer models or entirely new technology. These devices are still working, but they often have fewer features, diminished efficiency, manufacturer support is phased out, or they are incompatible with newer devices in their local device ecosystem. This poses challenges for maintenance, integration with other systems, and security. However, the lifecycle of these devices varies significantly. Legacy devices often lack major features that newer devices have. These features include: 1. Observability: Legacy devices that are not observable are replaced with new devices which offer this as a new feature. If the legacy device is already observable, a newer device might enable access in real-time, or integration with other systems. 2. Controllability: Legacy devices that are not controllable are replaced with new devices which support con- trol. If control was already possible, a newer device might offer additional control options and better control mechanisms. 2.1 Building System Devices Legacy devices can be grouped into a few different categories. Many of these devices are specific to a subset of building types as building size and purpose influence the choice of devices. 2.1.1 Thermal Equipment Thermal equipment is responsible for regulating the indoor air and water temperature. It encompasses HVAC equip- ment and water heaters. Each of these device types has a variety of subtypes, which are suited to different environ- ments and building types. • HVAC devicesinclude a wide breadth of equipment: furnaces, boilers, heat pumps, radiant heaters, Air Han- dling Units (AHU), Energy Recovery Ventilators (ERV), Heat Recovery Ventilators (HRV), exhaust fans and make-up air units, air conditioners, chillers, cooling towers, packaged Rooftop Units (RTU), Variable Refriger- ant Flow (VRF) systems, and Dedicated Outdoor Air Systems (DOAS). These devices are generally controlled by thermostats. The control complexity can range from simple on/off operation for single stage devices, to more complex controls that specify speeds or modulate output for multi-stage or variable speed equipment. Modern HVAC equipment can also integrate with Building Automation Systems (BAS) to enable energy- efficient operation, demand response, and optimization strategies that adjust performance based on occupancy, utility pricing, or grid conditions. • Water heatersfor both residential and commercial buildings can be either tankless or tank-based. Tankless water heatersprovide hot water on demand and typically require minimal control, though the desired out- put temperature can be set.
